lines.text: - moichaō (G3429) in the divorce/remarriage teaching: Matt 5:32's passive form describes a man's act (divorcing without cause) causing a third party (his wife) to be made an adulteress by her subsequent remarriage; Matt 19:9 and Mark 10:11 use the identical passive/deponent form for the remarrying party's own new status. Same morphology (passive voice), two different grammatical subjects bearing the consequence — one caused by another's act, two describing their own.

- moicheia (G3430, noun) as a vice-list item, listed among evil thoughts/theft/murder from the heart (Mark 7:21, Matt 15:19) — the abstract-state noun naming a category of heart-originating evil rather than a specific incident.

- moicheia's third occurrence names the specific narrative incident of the woman caught in the act (John 8:3), morph N-DSF — a dative of circumstance ('caught IN adultery'), the only occurrence naming a concrete event rather than an abstract vice-category.

- moicheuō in general reference: Rom 2:22's rhetorical double question (present active infinitive then present active indicative, confronting the hypocrisy of teaching against adultery while committing it) and Rev 2:22's substantive participle naming 'those who commit adultery with her' as a class following Jezebel's teaching — both using the verb to characterize ongoing conduct rather than a single event.

- porneia used relationally/identity-forming: 'we were not born of sexual immorality' (John 8:41, the Pharisees' claim of legitimate parentage) and 'she refuses to repent of her sexual immorality' (Rev 2:21, a named individual, Jezebel) — the noun tied to birth-legitimacy and to one person's persistent unrepentance, not a general category.

- porneia paired directly with idolatry in the death-list of vices to put to death (Col 3:5, 'covetousness, which is idolatry' — the same equation LSJ notes for the word itself: 'metaphorically, idolatry').

- na'aph (Qal perfect, 'dealt treacherously with you') Piel-adjacent to the figurative covenant-infidelity register: Hos 3:1's command to love an adulteress 'even as the Lord loves the children of Israel, though they turn to other gods' — this occurrence is the explicit hinge verse where the family's literal sense (marital infidelity) is stated in the same breath as its figurative application (Israel's idolatry), not merely implied by context elsewhere.

- niuph (H5004, noun) naming Jerusalem's 'adulteries and neighings, your lewd whorings' as a catalogued list of the city's own abominations (Jer 13:27), and describing a woman 'worn out by adultery' still being used as a prostitute (Ezek 23:43) — both occurrences concrete and disparaging, no figurative-idolatry sense stated explicitly within either verse itself (unlike na'aph's Hos 3:1).

- Matt 5:32 uses two different but closely related verbs for its two clauses: moichaō (G3429, 'makes her commit adultery' -- the caused-third-party sense) and moicheuō (G3431, 'commits adultery' -- the direct-agent sense for the man who marries the divorced woman), both morphologically V-APN (aorist passive infinitive) in the same verse. The verse deliberately varies between near-synonym roots to distinguish who is causing versus who is themselves committing the act.

- moicheuō as an aorist subjunctive negated prohibition ('do not commit adultery') in three separate commandment-list citations (James's 'whole law' argument, and two Synoptic commandment recitations) — a distinct grammatical register from both the future-indicative Decalogue formula above and Matt 5:28's completed-act aorist indicative: this is live moral instruction being given, not a quotation of a fixed legal text nor a statement about a past/completed inner act.

- na'aph as a finite or infinitive-absolute verb form, narrating a specific act rather than naming a person: a narrated historical event (Jer 29:23's 'they have committed adultery with their neighbors' wives'), an infinitive-absolute generic sin-listing (Hos 4:2, Jer 23:14, Jer 7:9, adultery catalogued alongside swearing/lying/murder/stealing), and Jeremiah's extended covenant-infidelity metaphor ('committing adultery with stone and tree,' Jer 3:9; 'they have committed adultery, and blood is on their hands,' Ezek 23:37).

- The aorist indicative at Matt 5:28 is meaning-critical, not incidental: Jesus's teaching depends on the tense specifically stating the act as already, completely done at the moment of the inward look — a present or future tense here would teach something weaker (that lust leads toward adultery, not that it already constitutes it). This is exactly the kind of morph-driven distinction round 1 had no rule requiring it to surface.

- James 2:11 itself carries two morphs of moicheuō in the same verse — an aorist subjunctive prohibition ('do not commit adultery,' repeating the command) and a present active indicative ('if you do not commit adultery but do murder') — the same verse shifts from quoting the command to describing the reader's actual, ongoing situation, marked by the tense/mood change alone.

- 1 Cor 10:8 carries porneuō twice with two different morphs in one verse: a present active subjunctive ('let us not indulge,' hortatory — the Corinthians' live, present temptation) and an aorist active indicative ('as some of them did,' the wilderness generation's completed past act) — the tense shift alone marks the boundary between the historical warning-example and the present exhortation it supports.

- Rev 19:2 and Col 3:5 both render porneia as bare 'immorality' rather than 'sexual immorality' — the ESV drops the 'sexual' qualifier at exactly the two points where the word is used most abstractly/metaphorically (Babylon's corrupting influence on the earth; a general vice-list entry next to 'impurity, passion, evil desire'), while every occurrence naming a concrete act or a named person keeps 'sexual.' The English surface itself is tracking the literal/metaphorical distinction, even though the underlying Greek word doesn't formally mark it.

- na'aph's Qal imperfect 2ms Decalogue citation ('you shall not commit adultery,' Exod 20:14, Deut 5:18) is the exact grammatical counterpart of this family's own Greek finding: G3431's future-active-indicative Decalogue citations (Matt 5:27, 19:18, Rom 13:9). Hebrew's imperfect-as-prohibition and Greek's future-as-imperative are each language's own way of grammaticalizing the same fixed commandment — a genuine cross-linguistic morph parallel, not merely a shared English translation choice.

- This family and family H_guilt (H0817) share the exact 'sin offering'/'guilt offering' vocabulary-conflation problem already noted there, but from a different angle: G3430's John 8:3 concrete-incident use and family H's Lev 5:7 offering-vocabulary overlap both show the English surface flattening distinctions the underlying source languages keep separate. Worth a joint review of surface-rendering consistency across the whole M10 cluster, not just within one family.

- John 8:3-4 uses both family members of this pair in adjacent verses for the same narrative incident: moicheia (G3430, the noun, 'caught IN adultery') at v.3, then moicheuō (G3431, the verb, perfect passive participle 'having been caught committing adultery') at v.4 -- the noun names the circumstance, the verb participle re-narrates the same woman's act as her defining state at the moment of accusation.
